ch10-newton-exact-for-quadratic: Section 10.2.1, p.540: follows at once from the definition of the step as the solution of the quadratic model and from the 10.1.1 KKT characterization; the book states it as an observation.
ch10-newton-step-feasible-descent-direct: Section 10.2.1, p.541: A dx = 0 is the second block equation, and descent follows from (10.14), which is a one-line consequence of (10.11) (use A dx = 0).
ch10-newton-affine-invariance: Section 10.2.1, pp.541-542: the book substitutes grad f-bar and the Hessian of f-bar into the KKT system and compares with (10.11) to get T dy = dx, w = w-bar.

ch10-newton-elimination-same-iterates-an: Section 10.2.3, pp.542-543: the book derives the reduced gradient and Hessian, verifies (10.16) via the nonsingular matrix, and shows the decrements equal; "defined iff" is a linear algebra fact from F^T H F.
ch10-convergence-assumptions: Section 10.2.4, p.544: the three assumptions (closed sublevel set, Hessian bounds and bounded KKT inverse, Lipschitz Hessian) are stated as the book's own.
ch10-infeasible-newton-step-defn: Section 10.3.1, p.546: (10.19) is obtained by linearizing the optimality conditions; it reduces to (10.11) when Ax = b.
ch10-infeasible-newton-is-primal-dual-st: Section 10.3.1, p.547: the book writes the derivative of the residual map r, gets (10.21)-(10.22), and shows they equal (10.19) with w = nu + dnu.
ch10-infeasible-newton-not-descent-for-f: Section 10.3.1, p.547: the book derives the directional derivative -dx^T H dx + (Ax-b)^T w from (10.19) and (10.23) from the residual map.
ch10-infeasible-damped-step-scales-resid: Section 10.3.1, p.548: r+ = (1-t) r from (10.24), then the product formula and the full-step consequence.
ch10-algorithm-infeasible-start-newton: Section 10.3.2, p.548: Algorithm 10.2 is the book's own algorithm, stated in full.
ch10-infeasible-line-search-terminates: Section 10.3.2, p.549: (10.23) gives a negative directional derivative of the residual norm, so the exit test holds for small t because alpha < 1/2; the feasible-coincidence follows from (10.24).
ch10-infeasible-start-cannot-detect-infe: Section 10.3.2, p.550: the book states a disadvantage of its own infeasible start method (no clear way to detect that no strictly feasible point exists; slow convergence before feasibility).
ch10-infeasible-basic-inequality: Section 10.3.3, pp.551-552: (10.28) is derived in full from the integral form, the Lipschitz condition and the bound K on Dr^-1, under the stated assumptions.
ch10-infeasible-damped-phase: Section 10.3.3, p.553: derived from (10.28) and the line search exit condition, giving the decrease alpha beta/(K^2 L) and the iteration bound.
ch10-infeasible-quadratic-phase: Section 10.3.3, p.553: derived from (10.28) at t = 1 and tmax > 1; a full step is taken and the squared recursion gives the stated rate.
ch10-infeasible-iterates-cauchy-optimal-: Section 10.3.3, pp.553-554: the book bounds the distance by 2K||r|| through the geometric sum, concludes the sequence is Cauchy and that r(y*) = 0 by continuity.
ch10-infeasible-newton-general-root-find: Section 10.3.4, p.554: the 10.3.3 proof uses only that r is differentiable, Dr is Lipschitz, Dr^-1 is bounded on the closed sublevel set, and the step Dr dy = -r; the book states the generalization with those conditions.
ch10-kkt-block-elimination-schur-negativ: Section 10.4.2, p.560: v = -H^-1(g + A^T w) and w = (A H^-1 A^T)^-1 (h - A H^-1 g) are derived by substitution; S = -A H^-1 A^T negative definite follows from H^-1 positive definite and rank A = p, elementary linear algebra.
ch10-kkt-block-elimination-structure-cos: coordinator sign-off, one rule across Boyd's parts (R3): Section 10.4.2, PDF p.560: the diagonal and banded totals come from substituting f and s for those structures into the itemized Algorithm 10.3 total. ch10-analytic-centering-three-methods-se: Section 10.4.3, p.562: states p = 100, n = 500, alpha = 0.1, beta = 0.5, four starting points, and shows (10.34) and (10.35) are p x p systems of the same cost; the infeasible start system is stated on p.562.
ch10-analytic-centering-initialization-r: Section 10.4.3, p.564: the requirements follow from the methods as the book defines them (feasible start, dual domain A^T nu > 0, x(0) > 0); the closing hedge is not a claim.
ch10-optimal-network-flow-structure: Section 10.4.3, p.565: the book defines the flow problem with the reduced incidence matrix (one redundant row deleted since the conservation equations sum to zero) and notes the two nonzeros per column.
ch10-lmi-analytic-center-dual-newton-cos: Section 10.4.3, p.568: the book itemizes the operations (forming gradient and Hessian, Cholesky) and sums them to 2pn^3 + (1/2)p^2n^2 + (1/3)p^3.
ch10-lmi-analytic-center-primal-block-el: Section 10.4.3, pp.568-569: the book linearizes (X+dX)^-1, eliminates dX to get (10.41), derives C w = d with C_ij = tr(A_i X A_j X), and itemizes the flop count; its leading terms match the dual's in order (the p^2 n^2 coefficient differs, 1 against 1/2).

ch11-interior-point-scope-barrier-primal: Section 11.1, p.575: the book says it concentrates on the barrier method with a convergence proof and complexity analysis, and describes a primal-dual method in 11.7 without analysis.
ch11-problems-in-scope-and-reformulation: Section 11.1, p.576: states which problem classes are already in form (11.1), shows the piecewise-linear to LP reformulation, and says SOCPs and SDPs are handled in 11.6; the statement is about what the chapter covers.
ch11-barrier-definition-and-indicator-ap: Section 11.2.1, p.577: the book defines I-hat_-(u) = -(1/t) log(-u); convexity, monotonicity, differentiability and closedness follow from the formula, and the accuracy statement is elementary calculus illustrated by Figure 11.1.
ch11-log-barrier-definition: Section 11.2.1, pp.577-578: phi(x) = -sum log(-f_i(x)) (11.5) with its domain is the book's definition; the blow-up near the boundary is immediate from the formula.
ch11-central-path-definition-and-conditi: Section 11.2.2, p.578: the book defines x*(t) as the solution of (11.6) (assumed unique for now) and gives the conditions (11.7), which are the optimality conditions of (11.6) from chapter 10.
ch11-lp-barrier-gradient-hessian: Example 11.1, p.579: the gradient A^T d and Hessian A^T diag(d)^2 A follow by calculus, d > 0 gives nonsingularity iff rank A = n, and (11.9) is (11.7) for the LP.
ch11-central-point-dual-feasible: Section 11.2.2, pp.579-580: the book shows lambda*(t) > 0, and that x*(t) minimizes the Lagrangian at (lambda*(t), nu*(t)), so g = f0(x*(t)) - m/t.
ch11-central-path-as-deformed-kkt: Section 11.2.2, p.581: substituting lambda_i = -1/(t f_i) in (11.7) gives (11.11), which differs from (11.2) only in the complementarity condition.
ch11-barrier-method-algorithm: Section 11.3.1, p.583: Algorithm 11.1 is the book's own, with its stopping rule m/t < epsilon and the SUMT history note.
ch11-barrier-outer-inner-iterations-feas: Section 11.3.1, p.583: outer and inner iterations are defined; the feasibility remark follows from the feasible-start Newton method and (11.10) at exact centering.
ch11-standard-form-lp-family-setup: Section 11.3.2, p.589: the book states n = 2m, N(0,1) entries of A, b = A x(0) with x(0) uniform on [0,1], c = A^T z + s, mu = 100, t(0) = 1, and the stop after the gap falls by 10^4 (two outer iterations).
ch11-barrier-centering-step-count: Section 11.3.3, p.591: after the initial step and k centering steps the gap is m/(mu^k t(0)); setting that at most epsilon gives (11.13), under the stated assumption that each centering problem is solved.
ch11-barrier-open-question-centering-dif: Section 11.3.3, p.591: the book states that its convergence analysis does not address whether centering gets harder as t grows; the numerical-evidence remark and the 11.5 resolution are given as suggestive, not as results.
ch11-centering-newton-step-is-modified-k: Section 11.3.4, p.592: the book writes (11.14) in terms of H and g and compares it with (11.17) to get v = dx_nt, nu = nu_nt/t; the primal-dual remark is a naming.
ch11-phase-i-purpose-and-problem: Section 11.4.1, p.593: the book defines phase I problem (11.19) and shows it is strictly feasible by choosing x(0) and s above max f_i(x(0)).
ch11-complexity-analysis-scope: Section 11.5, p.599: the book states what the self-concordance analysis covers (a bound on total Newton steps and a justification that centering does not get harder).
ch11-sqrt-m-mu-is-impractical: Section 11.5.3, p.606: the book states that mu = 1 + 1/sqrt(m) is far too small for practice and is of interest only because it approximately minimizes a very conservative bound.
ch11-feasibility-redundant-inequality-st: Section 11.5.4, p.607: the book bounds ||a|| <= mG/(s0 - F), so s0 = mGR + F gives ||a|| <= 1/R, and shows t(0) >= 1/(mGR) and a gap at most (m+1)mGR.
ch11-complexity-analysis-conservative-no: Section 11.5.6, p.609: the book states that its bounds are far above observed iteration counts and that it does not recommend the analysis's mu or the redundant inequality in practice; the remark on practical experience is context.
ch11-self-concordance-practical-advantag: Section 11.5.6, p.610: the book itself states it is not yet clear whether formulating a problem to satisfy self-concordance has a practical advantage.
ch11-sdp-barrier-and-duality-gap: Example 11.9, p.614. Gradient of log det is X inverse (derived in A.4.1). Optimality condition gives tr(F_i Z)+c_i=0 and Z positive definite directly, so no exercise is needed. Gap p/t follows from tr(X X inverse)=p. Gap value is stated by the general formula rather than computed line by line.
ch11-primal-dual-differences-from-barrie: Section 11.7, p.623. The bullets describe how the book's own primal-dual method is built (one loop, both variables updated, Newton on modified KKT, iterates not necessarily feasible). The similar-but-not-same claim is shown in 11.7.1.
ch11-primal-dual-search-direction-defn: Section 11.7.1, p.624. Delta y_pd is defined as the solution of (11.54). The feasible-direction remark follows from the third block row (A dx = -r_pri), shown in the text.
ch11-primal-dual-vs-barrier-matrix-struc: Section 11.7.1, pp.624-625. The elimination of d-lambda is shown, giving (11.55)-(11.56). Both H matrices are positive combinations of the same terms. The 1,1 blocks coincide when -f_i lambda_i = 1/t, as written in the displayed comparison.
ch11-surrogate-duality-gap-defn: Section 11.7.2, p.626. (11.59) defines the surrogate gap. The remark about t = m/eta follows from the gap m/t for central points.
ch11-sdp-diagonal-inequality-hessian: Section 11.8.3, p.633. With F_i = E_ii, H_ij = tr(S^-1 E_ii S^-1 E_jj) = (S^-1)_ij squared. The Hessian formula comes from the log det Hessian derived in A.4.3. Cost of forming S inverse is order n^3.
ch11-network-rate-optimization-problem: Section 11.8.4, pp.633-634. Problem (11.62) is the book's own formulation: separable concave nondecreasing utility, Ax <= c, x >= 0, with A the flow-link incidence matrix. Convexity is immediate.
appa-inner-product-euclidean-norm-defn: Appendix A.1.1, pp.647-648. Inner product, Euclidean norm, angle, matrix inner product are definitions. Cauchy-Schwarz is stated as standard background.
appa-norm-defn-and-unit-ball: Appendix A.1.2, p.648. Norm axioms are the definition. The unit-ball properties and converse are elementary and unmarked standard background.
appa-operator-and-dual-norm-defn: Appendix A.1.5-A.1.6, p.650. Operator norm and dual norm are defined. The max singular value, max-row-sum and max-column-sum identities are stated as standard background.
appa-interior-closed-sets-defn: Appendix A.2.1, pp.651-652. Interior, open, closed, closure, boundary are definitions. The sequence characterization of closed sets is standard analysis stated without a marker.
appa-supremum-infimum-conventions: Appendix A.2.2, p.652. These are the book's conventions for sup and inf, stated directly.
appa-function-notation-domain-convention: Appendix A.3.1, p.653. The notation f: A to B with dom f a subset of A is the book's own convention.
appa-closed-function-defn-and-criteria: Appendix A.3.3, pp.653-654. Closed function is defined by closed sublevel sets (equivalently closed epigraph). The criteria and Example A.1 are elementary analysis, stated unmarked.
appa-derivative-gradient-defn: Appendix A.4.1, pp.654-655. Derivative, first-order approximation and gradient are defined. Uniqueness of Df is a standard fact stated in a parenthesis.
appa-log-det-gradient-derivation: Appendix A.4.1, pp.655-656. The derivation is written out: factor X^{1/2}, eigenvalues of X^{-1/2} dX X^{-1/2}, log(1+lambda) approx lambda to first order, then trace identities. This is a textbook first-order argument, every step shown.
appa-chain-rule-first-derivative: Appendix A.4.2, p.656. The chain rule is standard calculus stated as background. The gradient and affine-composition corollaries follow by transpose and Dg = Df A.
appa-log-sum-exp-and-logdet-gradients: Examples A.2-A.3, p.657. Both gradients follow from the chain rule (A.5) and the derived gradient of log det (A.4.1). The steps are shown.
appa-hessian-and-second-order-approximat: Appendix A.4.3, pp.657-658. Hessian and second-order approximation are defined. The limit property is a standard calculus statement.
appa-log-det-hessian-derivation: Appendix A.4.3, p.658. The Hessian is derived from the first-order approximation of the gradient X inverse, via (I+A)^-1 approx I-A, giving the quadratic form -tr(X^-1 U X^-1 V). Steps are shown.
appa-second-derivative-chain-rules: Appendix A.4.4, p.659. (A.8) and the affine-composition rule follow by working out partial derivatives (standard calculus). Example A.4 applies them to log-sum-exp.
appa-eigenvalue-facts-definiteness: Appendix A.5.2, pp.660-661. Positive definite, semidefinite, matrix inequalities are defined. Eigenvalue-trace-determinant and Rayleigh facts are standard linear algebra stated unmarked.
appa-symmetric-squareroot-defn: Appendix A.5.2, p.661. A^{1/2} is defined through the eigenvalue decomposition. Uniqueness is standard linear algebra.
appa-generalized-eigenvalue-decompositio: Appendix A.5.3, p.662. Generalized eigenvalues and the decomposition (A.11) are defined, with the construction V = B^{1/2} Q shown from the standard decomposition.
appa-svd-defn-and-eigen-relation: Appendix A.5.4, p.662. The SVD is defined. The eigenvalue relation for A^T A is shown by direct substitution of (A.12).
appa-singular-value-facts-condition-numb: Appendix A.5.4, p.663. sigma_max, sigma_min and the condition number are defined. The supporting facts are standard linear algebra stated unmarked.
appa-pseudo-inverse: Appendix A.5.4, p.663. The pseudo-inverse is defined as V Sigma^-1 U^T. The limit forms and least-squares and projection properties are standard linear algebra stated unmarked.
appa-schur-complement-defn-and-determina: Appendix A.5.5, p.664. The Schur complement is defined. det X = det A det S is standard, and the block inverse formula is derived by elimination in the text.
appa-schur-complement-definiteness-chara: Appendix A.5.5, p.664. Minimizing the quadratic form over u by completing the square gives value v^T S v. The two definiteness criteria follow immediately from that.
appb-scope-two-quadratics: Appendix B, p.667. The book states the appendix covers problems with two quadratic, possibly nonconvex, functions.
appb-field-of-values-result: Section B.3, p.670. (B.8) is stated and proved by induction on rank with a rank-two construction (B.9). The convex cone remark follows because W(A,B) is the linear image of the PSD cone.
appb-field-of-values-proof-rank-two-case: Section B.3, pp.670-671. The rank reduction and both cases are written out: solving (B.9) via t^2+2t(z2-z1)=1 with one root satisfying 1+2t z1 > 0, and the collinear case. I checked the steps.
appc-scope-direct-methods: Appendix C, p.675. The book states it covers direct methods for linear equations and structure exploitation, and excludes numerical stability, factorization details, parallel and iterative methods.
appc-flop-definition-and-caveat: Appendix C.1.1, pp.676-677. A flop is defined, complexity is defined as the leading terms, and the book states the caveat about cache and locality for its own measure.
appc-basic-operation-flop-costs: Appendix C.1.2, p.677. Each count is derived in the text: inner product n multiplies and n-1 adds, matrix-vector 2mn from m inner products, matrix-matrix 2mnp, diagonal n, sparse 2N, factored 2p(m+n).
appc-forward-back-substitution-cost: Appendix C.2.1, pp.679-680. Forward substitution count 1+3+...+(2n-1) = n^2 is shown. The 2k n count for k nonzeros per row is shown step by step. Back substitution is the same.
appc-orthogonal-and-permutation-solves: Appendix C.2.1, p.680. x = A^T b costs 2n^2. For I-2uu^T, b - 2(u^T b)u costs 4n by counting. Permutation solves need no arithmetic by the book's flop definition.
appc-inverse-via-factor-solve: Appendix C.2.2, p.682. The inverse is obtained by solving A x = e_i for n unit vectors with one factorization, so cost is f+ns, by counting.
appc-inverse-cost-via-lu: coordinator sign-off, one rule across Boyd's parts (R3): Appendix C.3.1, PDF p.682: the inverse cost 8/3 n^3 is obtained by setting m = n in the derived m-right-hand-side cost (2/3)n^3 + 2mn^2 (factor once, then m solves). Moderately sure: the LU factor cost itself is only stated.
appc-block-elimination-schur: Appendix C.4.1, pp.686-688. Elimination (C.4)-(C.5) is derived. The block LU factorization in Remark C.1 is displayed. S nonsingular iff A nonsingular follows from A.5.5's determinant identity. The no-advantage point is shown in the (C.6) analysis.
appc-block-elimination-complexity: Appendix C.4.1, pp.688-689. Each of the four steps is counted and summed to (C.6). With f = 2/3 n1^3 and s = 2 n1^2 it equals 2/3 (n1+n2)^3. This uses the standard LU cost as background.
appc-matrix-inversion-lemma: Appendix C.4.3, p.692. The derivation by introducing y = Cx, eliminating x, and concluding for arbitrary b is written out. It implicitly needs I + C A^-1 B invertible.
appc-diagonal-plus-low-rank-cost: Appendix C.4.3, p.693. Both totals are built from itemized counts (2pn^2 + 2/3 n^3 against 2p^2 n + 2/3 p^3), with the standard LU cost as background. The comparison for p < n follows.
appc-sparse-plus-low-rank-cost: Appendix C.4.3, p.693. The itemized steps give f + (p+1)s + 2p^2 n + 2/3 p^3 (dropping lower terms), and the comparison with 2pn^2 + 2/3 n^3 follows when f and s are small.
appc-rank-one-update-cost: Appendix C.4.3, p.694. The update formula is derived from the inversion lemma and the cost f+2s follows by counting. Condition is 1 + v^T A^-1 u nonzero.
appc-underdetermined-solution-from-subma: Appendix C.5, p.695. The particular solution and the full parametrization are derived by elimination, and the costs f+s and f+s(n-p+1) follow by counting.
notation-function-and-derivative-convent: Notation, p.713. These are the book's own symbol definitions.
notation-generalized-inequality-symbols: Notation, p.712. These are the book's own symbol definitions.
notation-sets-and-matrix-symbols: Notation, p.711. These are the book's own symbol definitions.
duality-gap-certifies-suboptimality: Section 5.5.1, p.255. The bound p* >= g(lambda,nu) is proved in Section 5.1.3 (p.230, (5.2)). The epsilon-suboptimality, the interval and the zero-gap optimality follow in one line each.
weak-duality-lower-bound-holds-without-c: Section 5.2.2, pp.239-240. theory_low.ch3-second-order-strict-partial: Section 3.1.4, p.85: the second-order condition's proof is left to exercise 3.8, and the strict implication is stated with no proof. The x^4 counterexample is stated without checking strict convexity.
theory_low.ch3-quadratic-function-convexity: Example 3.2, p.85: rests on the second-order condition, whose proof the book leaves to exercise 3.8. The strict-convexity statement is 'easily characterized' with no proof.
theory_low.ch3-scalar-convex-function-examples: Section 3.1.5, p.85-86: the book says convexity of these 'can be shown' by (3.1) or by the second derivative and works only x log x. The second-order test it uses is exercise 3.8. The rest, including |x|^p and powers, is not shown.
theory_low.ch3-vector-convex-function-examples: Section 3.1.5, p.86-88: norms and max are proved directly (p.87). The quadratic-over-linear, log-sum-exp and geometric mean arguments use the Hessian test (second-order condition, exercise 3.8). The geometric mean Hessian is given only as a formula. log det rests on its own line argument.
theory_low.ch3-quadratic-over-linear-hessian: Section 3.1.5, p.87: the Hessian is written correctly, but convexity from a PSD Hessian is the second-order condition, left to exercise 3.8.
theory_low.ch3-log-sum-exp-convexity-proof: Section 3.1.5, p.88: the Hessian is stated (not derived) and its PSD check is by Cauchy-Schwarz; convexity from a PSD Hessian is the second-order condition, left to exercise 3.8.
theory_low.ch3-geometric-mean-concavity-proof: Section 3.1.5, p.88: the Hessian entries are given and the check is by Cauchy-Schwarz; concavity from a negative semidefinite Hessian is the second-order condition, left to exercise 3.8. The book says 'in a similar way'.
theory_low.ch3-geometric-arithmetic-mean-cone: Example 3.3, p.89: rests on concavity of the geometric mean G, whose proof (3.1.5) uses the Hessian test left to exercise 3.8. The superlevel step and homogeneity are elementary.
theory_low.ch3-jensen-finite-and-integral-forms: Section 3.1.8, p.91: the finite form is 'easily extended' and the infinite sum, integral and expectation forms 'extend'. Neither is proved in the book.
theory_low.ch3-jensen-characterizes-convexity: Section 3.1.8, p.91-92: the two-point random variable shows (3.5) implies (3.1), which gives the contrapositive. The value also says the inequality Jensen studied was the midpoint case, a historical statement about other work with no source.
theory_low.ch3-dithering-cannot-decrease-convex-val: Remark 3.2, p.92: follows from the expectation form of Jensen's inequality (3.5), which the book states without proof ('extends'). The remark itself is an interpretation.
theory_low.ch3-arithmetic-geometric-mean-via-jensen: Section 3.1.9, p.92: the derivation for sqrt(ab) <= (a+b)/2 is complete (-log convex, Jensen with theta=1/2, exponentiate). theory_low.ch3-piecewise-linear-convex-as-max-affin: Example 3.5, p.94: max of affine functions is convex (proved). The converse 'can also be shown' and is left to exercise 3.29.
theory_low.ch3-sum-of-r-largest-components-convex: Example 3.6, p.94: the unweighted sum is proved as a max of linear functions. The weighted version is 'it can be shown' and left to exercise 3.19.
theory_low.ch3-convex-function-supremum-of-affine-u: Section 3.2.3, p.97: the proof takes a supporting hyperplane to epi f at (x,f(x)); that is the supporting hyperplane theorem, which rests on the general separating hyperplane theorem left to exercise 2.22. The restricted-domain case is left to exercise 3.28.
theory_low.ch3-composition-extended-value-monotonic: Section 3.2.4, p.98: the general rules (3.11) are stated with the extension condition, but only one of the four cases is proved (p.99-100). The meaning of 'nondecreasing extension' is explained from the definition.
theory_low.ch3-simple-composition-results: Example 3.13, p.100: the results rest on the composition rules (3.11), of which only the convex/convex/nondecreasing case is proved. The 'log g concave' and '1/g convex' cases use other cases, left as 'similar'. The convexity of each h is not shown.
theory_low.ch3-vector-composition-second-derivative: Section 3.2.4, p.100: formula (3.15) is given, but the rules are 'we can derive many rules', not derived. They need the Hessian of a convex h to be PSD, which is the second-order condition left to exercise 3.8.
theory_low.ch3-vector-composition-extension-monoton: Section 3.2.4, p.101: the implication dom h - R+^k = dom h follows from the definition of a nondecreasing extension. theory_low.ch3-vector-composition-examples: Example 3.14, p.101: relies on the general vector composition rules, which are not proved, and states the convexity or concavity of each h without proof (log-sum-exp, p-norm, geometric mean).
theory_low.ch3-schur-complement-convexity-result: Example 3.15, p.102: the formula g(x)=x^T(A-BC^+B^T)x is stated with no derivation (pseudo-inverse, A.5.4). The conclusion A-BC^+B^T >= 0 needs convex quadratic implies PSD, which rests on the second-order condition (exercise 3.8).

value_replace.ch2-minimum-element-dual-proof: The book proves that x is the minimum element of S with respect to K if and only if for all lambda strictly positive in the dual order, x is the unique minimizer of lambda transpose z over S: for the converse, a point z in S that is not above x with respect to K yields a dual vector lambda tilde with negative product, and nearby strictly positive lambdas contradict uniqueness.
value_replace.two-way-partitioning-dual-sdp-lower-boun: For the two-way partitioning problem (5.7), which in general (for n larger than, say, 50) is very difficult to solve, the Lagrange dual function gives lower bounds on its optimal value. The dual problem is an SDP that can be solved efficiently even for n = 1000; its optimal value is a lower bound on the optimal value of the two-way partitioning problem, and is always at least as good as the lower bound (5.8) based on the smallest eigenvalue of W.
